body:
The task names three things that are easy to collapse into one — recurring disagreement about what an agreement meant, schedules that move, and a flatmate who has started avoiding the conversations — and the honest first move is to refuse the collapse. The earlier body already made this refusal explicit: it treated the later disagreements as a question with several live answers (memory gap, scope ambiguity, an unfair baseline load surfacing as chore talk), treated 'what would settled even mean here' as a separate question that nothing about the first question resolves, and treated the written record as a proposal aimed at the second question whose relevance depends on facts about this flat that the prose doesn't supply. I don't have new facts about the flat, and I won't invent them. What I can do is say more carefully what the situation looks like from where I'm standing, and where a next step would have to be anchored.

The most under-weighted feature in the task is the moving schedule. A flat where the load is stable and the agreements are stable is a different object from a flat where the people and their available hours change weekly. In the second flat, 'who does what' cannot be a fixed allocation without someone absorbing the mismatch, and the person who absorbs it will experience the agreements as vague or as renegotiated in bad faith even when nobody intended either. This is compatible with both the memory-gap reading and the scope-ambiguity reading, and it doesn't depend on any particular reading of the avoidant friend. It does mean that a probe asking only 'what did we agree this meant' can return answers that are really about availability, and I would want the probe to leave room for answers of the form 'I thought I'd do it Tuesday, but I'm not free Tuesdays anymore.' That is not a reinterpretation of the old agreement; it is a claim that the old agreement was made against a schedule that no longer holds.

The avoidant friend is the part of the task where I think the available prose is closest to right and also closest to overreach. The framing it proposes — ask for their view of the group conversations, not why they avoid them — is the smallest move that doesn't assume a mechanism. But I want to add a constraint that the earlier body mentions only as a risk: this move has to be made by someone who is willing to be one of the people whose own conduct is on the table. If the person who raises it is the person who currently holds the least load, or the most, the question will be heard through that fact. That isn't a reason to skip it; it's a reason to say out loud, when asking, that I am asking about the conversations as a whole and not about them. Whether that lands is testable: if the next group conversation happens and their participation is roughly what it was, the framing didn't obviously make things worse; if it stops entirely, I should treat that as evidence about how I raised it rather than as further evidence that they are the problem.

On the written record: I still treat it as a proposal, not advice, and I still think the falsifier the earlier body named is the right one — if writing down 'done' and the assignment leaves the recurring arguments intact, the memory-gap reading is at best incomplete. But I want to distinguish two ways a record can fail. It can fail because the disputes are actually about scope or load, in which case the record was addressing the wrong thing. And it can fail because a record of a now-stale agreement is more misleading than no record, since it freezes a division of labour into a text that the schedule has already invalidated. The second failure mode is the one I'd watch for here, because the schedule is the thing the task explicitly says changes.

What I won't do is turn this into a procedure with phases. The task asks what to do, and 'do this, then this, then this' would smuggle in a ranking of the readings that the material does not support. The nearest thing to a plan I'm willing to state is: ask the avoidant friend a question that doesn't presuppose why they avoid, in a way that includes me; try, if it survives that, to get from each flatmate a statement of what they currently think the last agreement was and what would make it not work now, with no scoring of whose answer is correct; and only then decide whether a written record is worth trying, knowing in advance that it might just relocate the dispute.

I also want to flag a way the earlier body could be misread. Its line that the probe's most likely outcome is uninformative is a claim about base rates in small flats, not a prediction about this one. If the probe does produce clustering answers, that is a real finding about this flat and should be treated as such. If it produces nothing, that is not evidence for the avoidance-as-central-mechanism reading; it is the absence of a finding, and the absence should not be promoted into a result.
commitments:
If this framing is taken up, the first thing that follows is a constraint on any probe or question, not a script: whatever gets asked should leave room for answers about availability and schedule, not only about what the old words meant. Someone acting on this would be committing to treat 'I'm not free that day anymore' as a live answer rather than as evasion. That is a real cost — it makes the probe harder to score — and it could be wrong if the actual disputes in this flat really are about wording rather than about time.

The second commitment is procedural and I want to state it as a proposal rather than as a recommendation: the move toward the avoidant friend is to be made by someone who is willing to include their own conduct in the question, and the person raising it should say so. If that is taken up, the failure mode to watch for is that the question lands as singling out or as a coalition move; the earlier body already flagged that risk, and I am keeping it as a cost, not as a reason to avoid the move. A reader who thinks this is too delicate a framing, or thinks a direct conversation about the avoidance is better, is disagreeing with a choice I am making rather than with a fact, and I don't have grounds to rule that out.

The third commitment relates to the written record. Acting on this framing means not treating the record as the intervention, and not ranking it above a mediator, a reallocation, or a formal household meeting; the earlier body's refusal to rank those is something I am retaining, and I would still retain it even if a probe did cluster around scope features, because clustering around scope makes a record's content different but doesn't by itself make a record the right next thing. If someone takes this up and the record turns out to fix the arguments, that would be evidence against my weighting of the schedule-staleness worry, and I would want that to count.

The fourth commitment is negative and easy to miss: the claim that the probe's likely outcome is uninformative is a base-rate remark, not a forecast about this flat, and it should not be used to pre-empt a finding. If answers do cluster, that is a finding; if they don't, that is an absence of a finding and should not be recorded as support for the avoidance reading. A reader who treats the absence as information is using the framing in a way I am explicitly disowning.

What I am not committing to: any reading of which of the three mechanisms (memory gap, scope ambiguity, baseline load) is correct here; any assumption that the avoidant friend's avoidance is a symptom rather than a response with its own reasons; and any procedure with an order of operations that would imply such a ranking. The most unresolved piece is whether asking the avoidant friend a non-presupposing question is compatible with also proposing a probe of past agreements — the two moves could interact, since the probe makes the past explicit at the moment the friend may be stepping back from group deliberation, and I don't know how that interaction would go. That is a live problem in this framing, not a hidden step I have already resolved.
